did_you_know.text: The exact location of Gerar is uncertain, but it is usually placed in southern Canaan, in the region south of Gaza.
The verb gur means to live somewhere temporarily, like a resident alien. Isaac is therefore told to stay in the land without yet treating it as his permanent home.

The story of a man presenting his wife as his sister also appears in the stories of Abraham in chapters 12 and 20. It is a recurring pattern in the patriarchal narratives, connected with fear of danger.
The phrase “a hundred measures” is commonly understood as a hundredfold harvest. During a famine, this describes extraordinary agricultural success.
Wells were essential in a dry region, not only for drinking but also for watering animals and raising flocks. Blocking them therefore threatened both livelihood and the ability to remain in the area.
Isaac restores the names Abraham gave to the wells. The names thus preserve memory and connect Isaac with the previous generation.
The name Esek is a play on the Hebrew root ע־שׂ־ק, associated with quarrelling or contending. The well’s name describes the conflict that arose over it.
Sitnah is related to the Hebrew root שט״ן, meaning opposition or hostility. This name also describes the treatment Isaac’s people received over the well.
Rehoboth is related to the Hebrew word for “wide” or “spacious.” After two conflicts, the name expresses relief and the chance to flourish.
The feast following the agreement is more than a meal; in the ancient world, eating together could express reconciliation and create a bond between the parties.
The name Beersheba plays on the similar-sounding Hebrew words sheva, “seven,” and shevuah, “oath.” It can therefore be understood as both “well of seven” and “well of an oath.”
The Hittites are mentioned in the Torah as one of the groups living in Canaan. Scholars debate whether they were directly connected with the larger Hittite Empire of Anatolia.
